title: Reading and Research
description: How to read for argument, remember what you read, judge sources and claims, search well, make usable notes, combine sources and cite them.
audience: A capable adult who reads a lot but has not been taught a method for reading, searching and citing. They know basic probability and can read a chart.
outcomes: You'll be able to choose how to read a text for a given purpose.
You'll be able to lay out an argument and find its assumption.
You'll be able to judge a source by reading laterally and a claim by its numbers and design.
You'll be able to build a search that finds what exists and follow its citations.
You'll be able to make notes you can reuse and combine them into a synthesis.
You'll be able to cite so that a reader can follow you.

lessons.title: Reading with a purpose
lessons.objective: Choose a reading approach for a stated purpose and estimate the time it will take.

concepts.title: Reading purpose
concepts.summary: The reason you are reading, which sets how deeply and in what order you read.

concepts.title: Survey
concepts.summary: A first pass over headings, abstract, first and last paragraphs and figures to learn the shape before reading closely.

concepts.title: SQ3R
concepts.summary: A study method: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review.

misconceptions: Reading every text from the first word to the last at one speed.
Believing a fast-reading technique can raise speed without lowering understanding.
Highlighting as a way of learning rather than a way of marking.
sequence: Ask the question before the page: why am I reading this?
Compare three purposes (find a fact, judge an argument, learn a method) and the pass each needs.
Walk through a survey of an article: title, abstract, headings, conclusion, then a decision.
Show SQ3R as a sequence and say why the question step comes before the reading.
Estimate reading time from length and speed.
examples: A 12,000-word article at 240 words per minute takes 50 minutes. A 300-page book at 25 pages per day takes 12 days. A survey of the abstract, headings and conclusion often takes a few minutes and tells you whether to read on.

figures.shows: Five SQ3R steps in a shuffled list.

questionPlan.sample: A 12,000-word article at 240 words per minute takes how many minutes?
A 300-page book at 25 pages a day takes how many days?
Put SQ3R in order: Recite; Survey; Read; Question; Review.

historyNotes: SQ3R is from Francis P. Robinson's Effective Study (1946). The 240 words per minute figure is an assumption for exercises.

lessons.title: Reading for argument
lessons.objective: Find the claim, the reasons and the evidence in a passage and state its unstated assumption.

concepts.title: Claim
concepts.summary: The statement an author wants you to accept.

concepts.title: Reason
concepts.summary: A statement offered to support a claim.

concepts.title: Warrant
concepts.summary: The assumption that links the evidence to the claim.

misconceptions: Taking the first sentence or the topic as the claim.
Reading a strong tone as strong evidence.
Missing the assumption because it is so plausible it passes unnoticed.
sequence: Show a short argument about street trees: 'Cities should plant more street trees. Shaded streets stay cooler in summer, so trees cut the number of heat-related illnesses.'
Mark indicator words (so, because, therefore) that point to reasons and conclusions.
Use the Toulmin parts to lay it out: claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal.
Find the unstated assumption: cooler streets mean fewer illnesses.
Test it by asking what would have to be true for the argument to fail.
examples: Claim: cities should plant more street trees. Grounds: shaded streets stay cooler. Warrant: cooler streets mean fewer heat-related illnesses. Qualifier added: 'in hot climates'. Rebuttal: unless trees' water use causes shortages.

figures.shows: The toulmin model with five statements drawn from the passage and their roles hidden.
figures.learnerAction: Assign each statement a role: claim, grounds, warrant, qualifier or rebuttal.

questionPlan.sample: In 'Cities should plant more street trees. Shaded streets stay cooler, so trees reduce heat illness', the claim is:
questionPlan.answer: Cities should plant more street trees
choices: Cities should plant more street trees

questionPlan.sample: The unstated assumption linking the grounds to the claim is:
questionPlan.answer: Cooler streets mean fewer heat-related illnesses
choices: Cooler streets mean fewer heat-related illnesses

questionPlan.sample: The assumption that links grounds to a claim is called the what?

lessons.title: Remembering what you read
lessons.objective: Use retrieval and spacing after reading and set a review schedule.

concepts.title: Retrieval practice
concepts.summary: Recalling information from memory, which strengthens it more than rereading.

concepts.title: Spacing
concepts.summary: Spreading reviews over time rather than massing them.

concepts.title: Illusion of fluency
concepts.summary: The feeling of knowing that comes from a familiar page, which does not show you can recall it.

misconceptions: Believing rereading and highlighting are the best ways to remember.
Taking an easy re-read as a sign of knowing.
Cramming a topic in one session and expecting it to last.
sequence: Close the book and write three sentences about what you just read, from memory.
Explain why that works: producing the answer strengthens the route to it.
Contrast with rereading and highlighting: familiar, but not recall.
Set spaced reviews after one, three, seven and fourteen days.
Add a weekly spoken summary of one book.
examples: Read on 3 November. Reviews after 1, 3, 7 and 14 days: 4 November, 6 November, 10 November, 17 November.

figures.shows: A calendar row from a reading day with review days to be filled in.

questionPlan.sample: Read on 3 November. A review 3 days later falls on which date in November?
A review 14 days after reading on 3 November falls on which date?
Rate your recall: write three sentences about the last chapter you read without looking.

historyNotes: Roediger and Karpicke (2006) 'Test-enhanced learning' is the usual cited study; check before quoting.

lessons.title: Kinds of source
lessons.objective: Classify a source as primary, secondary or tertiary, and scholarly, popular or trade, and say what each is good for.

concepts.title: Primary source
concepts.summary: Direct evidence made by participants or from original observation or data.

concepts.title: Secondary source
concepts.summary: An analysis of primary sources.

concepts.title: Tertiary source
concepts.summary: A summary of secondary sources, such as an encyclopaedia or textbook.

misconceptions: Believing peer-reviewed means correct.
Thinking a popular source is always unreliable.
Using an encyclopaedia as the end of research rather than its start.
sequence: Sort six items: an interview transcript, a journal article reporting an experiment, a review article, a textbook, a newspaper feature, a government data table.
Describe peer review and what it does and does not guarantee.
Explain preprints and retractions.
Match needs to sources: background, evidence, current figures.
Introduce open-access directories as a place to look.
examples: Interview transcript: primary. Journal article reporting a new experiment: primary (for the experiment). Review article: secondary. Textbook: tertiary. Government data table: primary data.

figures.shows: A sort grid with six items and three columns.
figures.learnerAction: Drag each item into primary, secondary or tertiary.

A journal article reporting the authors' own new experiment is:

lessons.title: Judging a source
lessons.objective: Apply lateral reading and the SIFT moves to an unfamiliar source and decide how far to trust it.

concepts.title: Lateral reading
concepts.summary: Leaving a page to see what others say about its source before reading the page closely.

concepts.title: SIFT
concepts.summary: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims, quotes and media to the original context.

concepts.title: Checklist
concepts.summary: A list of features such as date and author that is easy to apply and easy to fake.

misconceptions: Judging a website by its design or its About page.
Reading a page for a long time before checking who made it.
Treating a checklist as proof.
sequence: Describe a page from an organisation you do not know, with a professional design and an About page that sounds reputable.
Say what a checklist would conclude and why that is weak.
Show lateral reading: open a new tab and search for the organisation's name.
Walk through SIFT as four moves.
Decide: trust fully, trust for some things, or do not rely on it.
examples: A fictional site, the 'Institute for Healthy Living', publishes an article with a professional design. The SIFT order: stop and ask what you know, investigate the source by searching its name, find better coverage of the claim elsewhere, trace the claim to its original study.

questionPlan.sample: Order the SIFT moves: Trace; Stop; Find better coverage; Investigate the source.
questionPlan.answer: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace

questionPlan.sample: You land on an unfamiliar site with a polished About page. The best first move is:
questionPlan.answer: Search for the site's name in a new tab
choices: Search for the site's name in a new tab

questionPlan.sample: What does the S in SIFT stand for?

historyNotes: Caulfield's SIFT dates from 2019; the Stanford lateral reading study was reported in 2017 and 2019.

lessons.title: Judging a claim and its numbers
lessons.objective: Tell relative from absolute change, read a headline against the study design, and flag causal claims that a design cannot support.

concepts.title: Relative and absolute change
concepts.summary: Relative change compares the new rate to the old; absolute change is the difference.

concepts.title: Study design
concepts.summary: Whether the study assigned the exposure (an experiment) or only observed it.

concepts.title: Number needed to treat
concepts.summary: The number of people who must receive an intervention for one to benefit: 1 divided by the absolute reduction.

misconceptions: Taking 'halves the risk' as a large effect when the risk was tiny.
Reading correlation as causation from an observational study.
Trusting a number because it has many decimals.
sequence: Show a headline: 'New drug halves the risk of a rare event'.
Read the numbers: risk falls from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000.
Compute the relative reduction (50%), the absolute reduction (0.1 percentage points) and the number needed to treat (1,000).
Ask what design could support a causal claim.
Check the sample and who was in it.
examples: 2 in 1,000 is 0.2%; 1 in 1,000 is 0.1%. Relative reduction = 0.1 / 0.2 = 50%. Absolute reduction = 0.1 percentage points = 1 per 1,000. NNT = 1 / 0.001 = 1,000.

figures.shows: A before and after rate table with relative, absolute and NNT cells blank.

questionPlan.sample: Risk falls from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000. What is the relative reduction, in percent?
What is the number needed to treat?
'People who drink coffee live longer' from a survey of existing habits supports:
questionPlan.answer: An association, not proof of cause
choices: An association, not proof of cause

lessons.title: Searching well
lessons.objective: Turn a question into a search with synonyms, Boolean operators and filters, and extend it by following citations.

concepts.title: Boolean operators
concepts.summary: AND narrows a search, OR widens it and NOT excludes.

concepts.title: Truncation
concepts.summary: A wildcard that matches word endings, as in educat* for education and educator.

concepts.title: Citation chaining
concepts.summary: Following a source's references backward and the papers that cite it forward.

misconceptions: Typing the question as a sentence and reading the first page.
Stopping when the first search gives enough.
Using AND between synonyms, which narrows to nothing.
sequence: Start with a question and pull out its concepts.
List synonyms and spellings for each concept and join them with OR; join concepts with AND.
Use quotation marks for a phrase and an asterisk for endings.
Check the logic with counts.
Chain backward and forward from a good source.
examples: Set A has 100 results and set B has 80, with 30 in both. A AND B = 30. A OR B = 100 + 80 - 30 = 150. A NOT B = 100 - 30 = 70. Query: (teen* OR adolescen*) AND sleep AND "school start time*".

figures.shows: Two overlapping circles for sets A and B with counts hidden.
figures.learnerAction: Move the overlap slider and read AND, OR and NOT.

questionPlan.sample: A has 100 results, B has 80 and 30 are in both. How many results does A OR B return?
How many results does A NOT B return?
Which query is best for 'teenagers and sleep'?

lessons.title: Notes you can use later
lessons.objective: Write quotation, paraphrase, summary and comment notes, each with its source, and tell a true paraphrase from a copy.

concepts.title: Quotation
concepts.summary: Exact words, in quotation marks, with the page.

concepts.title: Paraphrase
concepts.summary: The idea in your own words and structure, with the source still cited.

concepts.title: Patchwriting
concepts.summary: Altering a few words of the original while keeping its structure, which is not a paraphrase.

misconceptions: Copying passages into notes without quotation marks and later mistaking them for your own words.
Thinking a paraphrase only needs synonyms.
Leaving the source out of a note.
sequence: Show an original sentence: 'Seedlings grown in low light stretch toward the window faster than those grown in bright light.'
Offer three versions: a quotation, a patchwriting, a paraphrase.
Say why one is patchwriting.
Add the source line to every note: author, year, page.
Separate your own comments from what the source says.
examples: Original: 'Seedlings grown in low light stretch toward the window faster than those grown in bright light.' Patchwriting: 'Seedlings raised in low light grow toward the window faster than ones raised in bright light.' Paraphrase: 'Plants kept in dim conditions reach for the glass sooner than brightly lit plants do.'

figures.shows: A note card template with fields for type, text, source, page and my comment.
figures.learnerAction: Fill in a card for a given passage.

questionPlan.sample: Which is patchwriting of 'Seedlings grown in low light stretch toward the window faster than those grown in bright light'?
questionPlan.answer: Seedlings raised in low light grow toward the window faster than ones raised in bright light
choices: Plants kept in dim conditions reach for the glass sooner than brightly lit plants do
Seedlings raised in low light grow toward the window faster than ones raised in bright light

questionPlan.sample: A note in your own opinion about a source is:
Exact words copied from a source must be put in what marks?

lessons.title: Combining sources
lessons.objective: Build a source matrix, find agreement, conflict and gaps, and write a synthesis that says more than any single source.

concepts.title: Synthesis
concepts.summary: A new statement built from several sources and organised by ideas, not by source.

concepts.title: Source matrix
concepts.summary: A table with sources in rows and questions in columns.

concepts.title: Vote counting
concepts.summary: Judging a question by how many sources agree, ignoring the size and quality of each study.

misconceptions: Summarising one source after another and calling it a synthesis.
Counting sources instead of weighing them.
Hiding conflict between sources.
sequence: Lay out five invented studies in a matrix.
Read across the rows for agreement and conflict.
Count participants rather than studies.
Write a synthesis: claim, support, conflict, gap.
Say what remains unknown.
examples: Five studies: n = 400, 250 and 120 find a benefit; n = 2,000 finds none; n = 90 finds harm. Total participants: 400 + 250 + 120 + 2,000 + 90 = 2,860. Three studies out of five favour benefit, but they include only 770 of 2,860 participants, so vote counting overstates the support.

figures.shows: A matrix of five invented studies against sample size and result.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the totals and mark which cells conflict.

questionPlan.sample: Total participants across the five studies (400, 250, 120, 2,000, 90)?
How many of the participants were in studies that found a benefit?
A paragraph that describes Source A, then Source B, then Source C is:
questionPlan.answer: A summary, not yet a synthesis
choices: A summary, not yet a synthesis

historyNotes: The studies in the example are invented for the exercise and should be labelled so.

lessons.title: Citing so a reader can follow
lessons.objective: Say what needs a citation, identify the parts of a reference, and spot citation errors.

concepts.title: Citation
concepts.summary: A pointer in the text to a source listed in full at the end.

concepts.title: DOI
concepts.summary: A persistent identifier that resolves to a published work.

concepts.title: Common knowledge
concepts.summary: A fact widely known and easily found in many sources, which needs no citation.

misconceptions: Citing only direct quotations.
Thinking a citation style is a matter of taste within one piece of writing.
Trusting a reference list produced by a tool without checking each item exists.
sequence: Ask why we cite: so a reader can find the source, and so the source gets the credit.
Decide what needs citing: quotations, paraphrases, data, distinctive ideas.
Break a reference into parts: author, year, title, container, volume, pages, DOI.
Compare styles (APA, MLA, Chicago) as different orderings of the same parts.
Check every reference against the source, including references suggested by a tool.
examples: A reference has author, year, title, journal, volume, pages and DOI. 'Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level' is common knowledge. A statistic from a survey is not.

figures.shows: A reference with parts labelled by colour and one part missing.

questionPlan.sample: Which needs a citation?
choices: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level

questionPlan.sample: A DOI is:
questionPlan.answer: A persistent identifier that resolves to a published work
choices: A persistent identifier that resolves to a published work

questionPlan.sample: A reference suggested by an AI tool names a paper you cannot find in any database. You should:
questionPlan.answer: Treat it as unverified and not cite it
choices: Treat it as unverified and not cite it

historyNotes: Citation styles evolve; the writer should check the current editions of APA, MLA and Chicago before quoting rules.

courseCheck: A mixed set: order SQ3R and the SIFT moves; estimate reading time; find claim and warrant; schedule reviews; classify sources; compute relative and absolute reduction and the number needed to treat; compute Boolean result counts; identify patchwriting; weigh studies by participants; decide what to cite and read a reference.
platformNeeds: source_card figure: a source extract with its provenance (author, date, publisher) and a hidden panel for each SIFT move that the learner opens in order. Fallback: table plus order_sequence.

search_simulator: a small fixed library of records on which the learner builds Boolean queries and sees result counts update, with overlap shown as a Venn view. Fallback: the svg_figure of overlapping circles in lesson 7.
note_card editor: not a figure; practice of note-making is by choice and recall questions only, since free-text marking is not available.
Matrix figure with editable cells and column totals for lesson 9 (the table figure covers display only).
unverified: The 240 words per minute figure is an exercise assumption; published averages vary by text and reader.
Roediger and Karpicke 2006 as the source of the test-enhanced learning effect.
The Wineburg and McGrew lateral-reading study (2017 report, 2019 article) and Caulfield's SIFT (2019).
The licences of the Caulfield works (CC BY 4.0), OpenStax Writing Guide (CC BY 4.0), Zotero documentation, and the Crossref documentation, from memory.
The five studies in lesson 9 and the site in lesson 5 are invented for the course and must be labelled as invented.
Current citation style editions (APA, MLA, Chicago) were not checked.
No source was opened (external hosts were blocked); every source is marked verified false.
